    Front-panel practice and model limits

    WAVE cycles sine, square and triangle. Enter a frequency, then SHIFT → 8 / 9 / 0 for MHz / kHz / Hz. SHIFT → 4 / 5 chooses the frequency-knob digit. SHIFT → decimal switches V/F display. SHIFT → 3 toggles −40 dB. Enable OUTPUT before SHIFT → WAVE for TTL. Push DUTY to reset 50%; push OFFSET to remove its DC contribution. Power-up restores sine / 1 kHz and leaves output off in this trainer.

    Preset loading may start with output enabled. The extra readouts and load checkbox below the chassis are teaching aids, not hardware controls. MAIN is modeled as a clipped voltage source with 50 Ω series resistance; its display uses nominal peak-to-peak voltage into 50 Ω. TTL uses an ideal 0–5 V waveform (the manual specifies ≥3 Vpp); TTL loading, edge timing, noise, accuracy and warm-up are not modeled. Duty adjustment is limited to ≤1 MHz. TTL and MAIN are separate leads with a common grounded return; the trainer retains the MAIN waveform while TTL is enabled and mutes triangle MAIN above 1 MHz.

    4. Instructor / student notes

    Build and measure

    Connect MAIN and GEN return. Put CH1 at the filter input and CH2 at its output, with all ground clips on the return. For a single sine wave, change generator frequency manually and calculate gain = CH2 Vpp / CH1 Vpp. For output phase relative to input, select Phase with Source 1 = CH2 and Source 2 = CH1; a lag is negative. A mixed signal does not have one frequency gain or phase: its Vpp ratio describes the whole waveform, not each component. The 50 Ω generator amplitude convention differs from an ideal voltage source: measure Vin with CH1.

    Filter a synthetic signal

    The Source selector is available without unlocking presets. Build a high-pass circuit to preserve 200 Hz UAV motor vibration while reducing slow aircraft movement at 2 and 5 Hz, or a low-pass circuit to reduce fast interference in the sensor example. The UAV task is to preserve at least 95% of the vibration, reduce 2 Hz movement below 5%, and reduce 5 Hz movement below 15%. A 33 kΩ resistor and 100 nF capacitor give a cutoff near 48.2 Hz. Increasing cutoff rejects more movement but eventually weakens useful vibration.

    Source selection keeps your circuit and scope settings. Press Autoset after loading the UAV vibration high-pass preset, or set DC coupling and both channels to 0.5 V/div manually. Use 100 ms/div to reveal aircraft movement, then 2 ms/div to inspect motor vibration. Autoset also works with the sensor example and recalled Legacy EEG signals.

    • Breadboard connectivity and user-created jumper wiring.
    • Ideal resistors and capacitors wired to independent, initially unpowered breadboard rails. MAIN includes the generator’s 50 Ω source resistance.
    • Two oscilloscope probes referenced to common instrument ground. CH1 and CH2 share the same instrument ground in the real scope, so mismatched grounds are flagged.
    • RC response to the generator waveform or a repeatable synthetic signal mixture. A circuit that exceeds the numerical budget reports an unavailable calculation instead of a guessed trace.
    • Oscilloscope vertical/horizontal scale, coupling, position, trigger source/slope/level/mode, sample/average/peak acquire modes, channel-colored cursors, automatic measurements with gating and statistics, arithmetic math, run/stop, single, autoset, save/recall, and help.

    What is deliberately simplified

    • This is a training simulator, not a SPICE replacement and not a manufacturer firmware emulator.
    • Serial-bus decode, LAN/USB remote control, Go/NoGo hardware I/O, printer/PictBridge behavior, and calibration procedures are represented in the UI but not electrically emulated.
    • Resistors and capacitors are ideal. No tolerances, parasitics, dielectric effects, or scope input loading are modeled.
